consensus_summary: The white horse principally signifies victory or conquest. Revelation 19 clearly presents Christ’s righteous triumph, while Revelation 6 depicts conquest but leaves the rider’s identity disputed; horses more generally signify military power or divinely commissioned action.
book_summary: The entry restricts the image to Revelation 6:2: the white horse is the mount of an executing spiritual agent, whose rider conquers nations by means of the bow.
consensus_core_identification: White horse imagery signifies victorious conquest or triumphant power.
book_core_identification: The Revelation 6 white horse is the mount of a bow-bearing spiritual executor engaged in conquest.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus covers white-horse imagery broadly, including Christ’s victory in Revelation 19 and several disputed interpretations of Revelation 6. The book selects the Revelation 6 case and specifies an executing spirit and bow-based conquest, thereby excluding the wider range of white-horse cases and interpretations.
material_contradiction: There is no direct contradiction at the core: both identify conquest. The book does not expressly reject Christological, generic-conquest, or other readings, but its narrow definition does not encompass them.
rationale: Reduced to their minimum cores, both readings identify the white horse with conquest. The book materially narrows that shared category to the bow-bearing conqueror of Revelation 6 and further characterizes the rider as an executing spirit. That spiritual-agent specification is recognizable within consensus references to divinely commissioned agents, so it is neither divergent nor wholly novel.
strongest_objection: Revelation 6:2 directly supports the bow, crown, and conquest, but it does not identify the rider as a spirit or explicitly state that the conquered objects are nations. Those elements require interpretation beyond the printed citation.
